newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Bidders submit Thomson privatisation offers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bidders submit Thomson privatisation offers.

text.p: France's Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere Groupe on Monday both submitted their bids to the government to acquire electronics and defence group Thomson SA, a Finance Ministry spokesman said.
The government is expected to decide at the end of this month or early October which of the two companies will get the green light.

Alcatel, the industrial conglomerate headed by Serge Tchuruk, has conducted a silent campaign to win backers in the government for its offer to buy all of Thomson, both the loss-making Thomson Multimedia consumer electronics arm as well as the 58-percent-owned Thomson-CSF defence electronics company.

Lagardere, in contrast, has been waging a more public campaign for its offer which foresees it obtaining at least a 60 percent stake. Lagardere, which owns Matra, is mainly interested in the defence electronics activities, together with its ally British Aerospace Plc.

Korea's Daewoo Electronics would obtain control over the multimedia activities, which include such brands as Saba and RCA. Daewoo's president Bae Soon Hoon told the Les Echos newsppaer on Monday that he aimed to make the activities profitable in two years' time.

Noel Forgeard, the chairman of Lagardere's defence and space activities, said that the assets of Matra would be transferred to Thomson-CSF to create Thomson-Matra which would remain listed on the Paris Bourse. BA could hold five percent in Thomson-Matra and Thomson staff between five to six percent.

For the government, and President Jacques Chirac, there are a number of key questions that will decide who will win. Neither of the two bids will raise much money for the state due to the multimedia losses -- incurred because of heavy investments in new technologies at a time of rapid market changes.

Thomson Multimedia lost three billion francs ($581 million) in the first half of 1996 and is reported to be planning a restructuring including 5,000 job losses, out of a work force of 49,500, mainly outside France.

Thomson SA chairman Marcel Roulet will want to make sure the future of the company is assured and that a takeover bid makes industrial sense. With French unemployment standing at over 12 percent, the goverment is unlikely to favour a plan which foresees big job losses in the near future.

Another issue is the restructuring of the French, and European, defence industry. The Lagardere bid would bring Thomson-CSF into the Matra-British Aerospace sphere and further consolidate the industry.
Chirac himself is pushing a restructuring of the defence industry and has been orchestrating the planned merger of Aerospatiale and Dassault Aviation.

If Alcatel won the bidding, alliances for Thomson-CSF are not excluded and some analysts expect Britain's GEC Plc to become involved. GEC is Alcatel's partner in the giant GEC-Alsthom NV industrial power and high speed trains joint venture which recently obtained permission to acquire nuclear engineering group Framatome from the French state.

Alcatel said in the past it would keep Thomson Multimedia. This would allow Alcatel to gain an entry into consumer markets which can be practical for its portable telephone products and future personal communciations equipment.

The Alcatel bid would keep France's last remaining television annd videorecorder company in French hands while not excluding future deals with other European consumer electronics makers -- such as Philips Industries NV and Siemens AG -- or existing partners such as Sharp Corp.
